title: Too small for the console war, too early for the streaming box
lede: Ouya reached stores five months before the PlayStation 4 and nine months before Amazon put games on a $99 television box. The other Android micro-consoles that shared its store were switched off on the same day it was.

blocks.title: Sony sold in a day about 16 times what Ouya’s campaign drew in a month

left.label: PlayStation 4 consoles sold in North America in the first 24 hours, by Sony’s count[^19]

unit.label: backers of the Ouya Kickstarter over 30 days[^1]

blocks.equation: 1,000,000 ÷ 63,416 = 15.8, rounded up to 16 icons. Each icon stands for one Ouya campaign’s worth of backers. Backers are not console sales; Ouya never published those.
blocks.source: Sony Computer Entertainment press release, November 17, 2013[^19]; Kickstarter[^1].

blocks.title: Boxes for the television, 2013 to 2015
blocks.subtitle: What each one was, and what became of it.

items.name: Ouya
items.text: June 2013. Sold to Razer without its hardware in 2015.[^10][^25]

items.name: Mad Catz M.O.J.O.
items.text: Price as of July 2014, when it became the first outside device to carry the Ouya store. Its store closed with Ouya’s.[^22][^30]

items.name: Razer Forge TV
items.text: Razer’s own Android TV console, the intended home for Ouya’s users and games. 9to5Google says it was on the market for a matter of months.[^25][^32]

items.name: Amazon Fire TV
items.text: April 2014, with games from EA, Disney and others and a $39.99 controller.[^20]

items.name: PlayStation 4
items.text: November 15, 2013 in the United States and Canada.[^19]

blocks.source: Company press releases[^19][^20][^22][^25], Razer’s shutdown notice[^30] and 9to5Google[^32]. The sparkline for Ouya is the home-page game counter[^34], not sales. We have no launch price for the Forge TV in our sources.
